Sensors give your robot perception.

Color sensors detect RGB values (0-255 each). The simulator has a virtual color sensor built into most robot models.

In loop(), display readings: telemetry.addData("Red", colorSensor.red());

Do the same for green() and blue(). Each returns 0-255.
(255,0,0)=red, (0,255,0)=green, (0,0,255)=blue, (255,255,0)=yellow. The sensor reads whatever is in front of it.

An IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) is a sensor that measures the robot's heading — which direction it's pointing.

It combines a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer into one chip (like the BNO055 on the Rev Expansion Hub or the built-in IMU on the Control Hub).

The gyroscope measures angular velocity — how fast the robot is turning. By integrating this over time, the IMU tracks heading.

The accelerometer measures linear acceleration — including gravity. It tells the IMU which way is down, giving a gravity reference.

The magnetometer acts like a compass, measuring the Earth's magnetic field to determine absolute orientation.

All three are fused together to produce a single clean heading value that doesn't drift over the course of a match. This is critical for localization — without an IMU, dead wheels alone can't reliably track heading.

Declare a private GyroSensor field. In init(), get "gyro_sensor" from hardwareMap:

gyroSensor = hardwareMap.gyroSensor.get("gyro_sensor");

Call gyroSensor.calibrate() right after to zero the heading.

In loop(), call gyroSensor.getHeading() — it returns heading in degrees from -180 to 180.

Display it with telemetry.addData("Heading", heading).

Now start the OpMode and rotate the robot by clicking and dragging. Watch the heading change.

0 degrees = the direction the robot was facing when you calibrated.

Positive angles = counter-clockwise rotation.

Negative angles = clockwise rotation.

-180 and +180 are the same direction.

The IMU gives you absolute heading. Unlike encoder-based heading estimates (which drift), the IMU stays accurate because it has an absolute gravity reference and magnetometer.

This is why localization systems fuse IMU heading with dead wheel odometry — the dead wheels track position, the IMU tracks orientation.
